MRI__Brain:
A routine brain MRI is not one image but a stack of sequences, each weighting tissue differently so that pathology which is invisible on one appears obvious on another. Reading a scan means knowing what each sequence makes bright and what it makes dark, then combining them into a diagnosis. MRI has no ionising radiation and vastly superior soft-tissue contrast than CT.
1T1 vs T2 — the physics intuition
Weighting is set by the TR (repetition time) and TE (echo time). T1-weighted images show anatomy best: CSF is dark, white matter is brighter than grey, and fat and subacute blood (methaemoglobin) are bright. T2-weighted images make fluid and oedema bright, so most pathology lights up. The classic aide-memoire: “WW2 = Water is White on T2.” If CSF in the ventricles is bright, you are looking at T2; if it is dark, T1.
T1 fat/subacute blood bright, CSF darkT2 water/oedema/most pathology bright
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: side-by-side axial T1 and T2 of the same slice, showing ventricular CSF dark on T1 and bright on T2 to anchor the “WW2” rule.
2FLAIR and the diffusion pair (DWI/ADC)
FLAIR is a T2 sequence with the CSF signal suppressed (nulled) so it appears dark like on T1, while oedema and gliosis stay bright. This makes periventricular and cortical lesions stand out instead of being masked by adjacent bright CSF — it is the workhorse for MS plaques and small ischaemic change. DWI detects restricted diffusion: a bright DWI signal that is correspondingly dark on the ADC map confirms true restriction (avoiding “T2 shine-through”).
DWI bright + ADC dark→acute infarct (earliest sign, positive within minutes)
Restricted diffusion, non-vascular territory→think abscess, or hypercellular tumour (e.g. lymphoma)
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial DWI showing a wedge of bright restricted diffusion in a middle cerebral artery territory, with the paired ADC map showing corresponding low signal, confirming acute infarct.
3GRE/SWI and post-gadolinium T1
GRE/SWI (susceptibility-weighted) is exquisitely sensitive to blood products, microbleeds and calcium, which “bloom” as dark foci — used for haemorrhagic transformation, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cavernomas and diffuse axonal injury. Post-gadolinium T1 shows where the blood–brain barrier has broken down: contrast leaks and enhances in tumour, infection and inflammation. Enhancement patterns are diagnostic — a ring-enhancing lesion raises abscess, glioblastoma or metastasis.
🧲GRE / SWI
Blood, microbleeds and calcium bloom dark
💉Post-Gad T1
BBB breakdown: tumour, infection, inflammation enhance
4When to choose MRI over CT
CT is faster and better first-line for acute haemorrhage and trauma, but MRI wins wherever detail and soft tissue matter. Prefer MRI for the posterior fossa and brainstem (CT beam-hardening artefact obscures this), the spinal cord, multiple sclerosis, small tumours and metastases, and the seizure/epilepsy work-up (hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia). MRI also detects acute infarction far earlier than CT via DWI.
Posterior fossaCordMSSmall tumoursSeizure work-up
🚩
MRI safety is life-critical. The magnet is always on. Screen every patient for ferromagnetic implants, older/non-conditional pacemakers and ICDs, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and, crucially, intra-orbital metallic foreign bodies (ask about metalwork/grinding history — a fragment can move and blind the patient). Loose ferromagnetic objects become deadly projectiles. Gadolinium can precipitate nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) in severe renal impairment — check eGFR before contrast.
🎓 Exam pearl. DWI is the earliest imaging sign of acute stroke — bright on DWI with matching dark ADC positive within minutes, long before CT changes. Remember DWI can shine bright from T2 shine-through, so always confirm true restriction against the ADC map.
In suspected acute ischaemic stroke, MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the single most sensitive test — it lights up an infarct within minutes, long before CT shows anything. Understanding why comes down to one idea: dying neurons stop pumping ions, water floods into cells (cytotoxic oedema), and that trapped water can no longer diffuse freely.

1THE PHYSICS: WHY DWI IS BRIGHT AND ADC IS DARK
DWI measures how freely water molecules move. Normally water diffuses freely and the DWI signal decays — appearing relatively dark. In acute ischaemia, failure of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump causes water to shift intracellularly (cytotoxic oedema), so diffusion is restricted. Restricted water retains signal, so the infarct is DWI BRIGHT. Critically, DWI alone can mislead because of T2 shine-through (a bright T2 lesion looking bright on DWI without true restriction). The ADC map resolves this: true restriction is ADC DARK (low). Bright DWI + dark ADC = true diffusion restriction = acute infarct.
DWI bright AND ADC dark→true restriction — acute ischaemic core
DWI bright BUT ADC bright→T2 shine-through — NOT acute restriction
2THE TIMELINE: DWI–FLAIR MISMATCH DATES THE STROKE
Signals evolve predictably, and this lets MRI act as a clock. DWI becomes positive within minutes. FLAIR/T2 changes lag, only becoming visible after roughly 4.5–6 hours. Therefore a lesion that is DWI positive but FLAIR negative — the DWI–FLAIR mismatch — implies the stroke is likely <4.5 hours old. This is decisive in wake-up stroke or unknown onset time: mismatch supports offering thrombolysis even when the clock is uncertain. Over days the ADC pseudonormalises (rises back through normal ~7–10 days, so a subacute infarct can have a falsely normal ADC), while T2/FLAIR become brightly positive.
DWI+ / FLAIR− = likely <4.5 hDWI+ / FLAIR+ = probably >4.5 hADC pseudonormalises ~7–10 days
📷 Image placeholder — side-by-side DWI and FLAIR of the same slice showing a bright DWI lesion with a still-normal (negative) FLAIR — the classic DWI–FLAIR mismatch of a hyperacute infarct.
3TERRITORIES, LACUNES AND WHERE CT FAILS
DWI localises the lesion to a vascular territory, which predicts the clinical syndrome. MCA: contralateral face/arm weakness, aphasia (dominant), neglect. ACA: contralateral leg weakness. PCA: homonymous hemianopia. A small deep round lesion in the internal capsule, basal ganglia or pons is a lacunar (small-vessel) infarct, versus a larger cortical/wedge-shaped territorial infarct from large-vessel or embolic disease. DWI is invaluable in the posterior fossa (brainstem/cerebellum), where CT is degraded by bone artefact and small infarcts are easily missed. It also confirms tissue injury in TIA workup (a DWI lesion means true infarction and higher recurrence risk).
🧠MCA infarct
Face/arm weakness, aphasia or neglect; large cortical DWI territory.
🦵ACA infarct
Contralateral leg-predominant weakness; medial frontal territory.
👁️PCA infarct
Homonymous hemianopia; occipital DWI lesion.
🔴Lacunar
Small deep round infarct (capsule/pons); pure motor/sensory syndrome.
4HAEMORRHAGE AND THE RESTRICTION MIMICS
MRI is not blind to blood: GRE and especially SWI sequences are exquisitely sensitive to haemorrhage and microbleeds, showing blooming low signal. This matters because thrombolysis is contraindicated if there is bleeding. Finally, remember DWI restriction is not 100% specific for infarction — a short differential includes a cerebral abscess (restricting pus centrally, with a ring-enhancing wall) and hypercellular tumours (e.g. lymphoma, high-grade glioma). Clinical context and lesion shape usually distinguish these from a vascular-territory infarct.
🚩
MRI must never delay time-critical reperfusion. In the hyperacute pathway a non-contrast CT head is done first to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis — it is fast and universally available. Do not send an unstable patient into a slow MRI when the therapeutic window is closing. Remember MRI contraindications: pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, certain metallic foreign bodies and unstable/monitored patients.
🎓 Exam pearl. "DWI bright + ADC dark = acute infarct" is the highest-yield line. Add the timing hook: DWI positive with FLAIR still negative ⇒ stroke likely <4.5 h, which lets you thrombolyse a wake-up/unknown-onset stroke. But in the emergency door-to-needle pathway, CT head first to exclude bleed — MRI never delays reperfusion.

MRI is the single most important investigation in diagnosing multiple sclerosis. It demonstrates the characteristic demyelinating plaques, allows the McDonald criteria to be applied (dissemination in space and time), distinguishes active from old lesions, and is the mainstay of monitoring disease activity and treatment response. Reading an MS brain MRI is a core clinical skill.

1What an MS plaque looks like

MS plaques are focal areas of demyelination. On MRI they are T2/FLAIR hyperintense (bright) white-matter lesions. FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) suppresses the bright CSF signal, making periventricular lesions stand out — it is the key sequence for lesion detection. On T1 imaging, chronic severe lesions appear as hypointense "black holes", marking axonal loss and irreversible damage.

T2/FLAIR: bright plaques — lesion load / "where"
T1 + gadolinium: enhancement = active; black holes = old damage
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Axial FLAIR brain: multiple ovoid periventricular hyperintense lesions abutting the lateral ventricles, several oriented perpendicular to the ventricular margin (Dawson fingers). Highlight the callososeptal interface.
2Where the lesions live — the four typical locations

MS has a strong predilection for four white-matter territories. Recognising these underpins "dissemination in space".

🧠Periventricular
Ovoid lesions abutting ventricles; Dawson fingers radiate perpendicular to the corpus callosum along deep medullary veins — best seen on sagittal FLAIR.
🧩Juxtacortical
Lesions touching the cortex (subcortical U-fibres). Involvement of the grey-white junction is fairly specific for MS.
🌐Infratentorial
Brainstem (esp. pons, middle cerebellar peduncles) and cerebellum. Often causes prominent clinical signs (diplopia, ataxia).
🦴Spinal cord
Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, often cervical cord. Contrast with longitudinally extensive lesions of NMOSD.
3McDonald criteria — space and time

Diagnosis requires objective evidence of demyelination disseminated in space (DIS) and in time (DIT).

≥2 of the four typical locations involved→Dissemination in SPACE satisfied
New lesion on follow-up scan, OR simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing + non-enhancing lesions on one scan→Dissemination in TIME satisfied

A single scan can therefore establish MS if it shows lesions in ≥2 typical sites and both an enhancing and a non-enhancing lesion. CSF oligoclonal bands can now substitute for DIT in some criteria versions.

4Gadolinium — active vs old

Gadolinium does not cross an intact blood–brain barrier. In acute demyelination the BBB breaks down, so contrast leaks into the lesion.

Lesion enhances with gadolinium→Active/acute (BBB breakdown, typically enhances for ~2–6 weeks)
Lesion does not enhance→Old/inactive lesion

An open-ring (incomplete rim) enhancement pattern, with the open edge toward grey matter, is characteristic of demyelination and helps distinguish tumefactive MS from abscess or tumour.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Post-gadolinium T1 axial: one white-matter lesion showing incomplete open-ring enhancement alongside a non-enhancing hypointense "black hole" — illustrating simultaneous active and chronic lesions (DIT on a single scan).
5Optic neuritis, DDx and chronicity

Optic neuritis is a common presenting event — painful monocular visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect; MRI with fat-suppressed orbital sequences shows an enhancing, swollen optic nerve. It is a clinically isolated syndrome that frequently converts to MS.

Differential of white-matter lesions:

Small-vessel ischaemia: older/vascular risk patients, subcortical + basal ganglia, spares corpus callosum, no enhancement
ADEM: monophasic, post-infectious, large confluent lesions all enhancing at once (same age)
Migraine: small punctate deep white-matter dots, non-specific
Vasculitis / SLE: multifocal, may enhance, look for infarcts and systemic features

Chronicity markers: confluent "black holes", and progressive brain and cord atrophy (thinning corpus callosum, widened ventricles) reflect accumulated neurodegeneration.

6Monitoring disease and treatment

Serial MRI tracks disease activity even when the patient is clinically stable. New/enlarging T2 lesions or new enhancing lesions indicate ongoing inflammatory activity and may signal inadequate disease-modifying therapy. A rebaseline scan is performed after starting or switching treatment so future scans have a comparator. "NEDA" (no evidence of disease activity) incorporates absence of new MRI lesions.

🚩MRI supports but does not alone prove MS — actively exclude mimics and red-flag features. Findings that make MS unlikely include: normal MRI with progressive symptoms, longitudinally extensive cord lesions (think NMOSD/aquaporin-4), meningeal enhancement, symmetrical confluent leukodystrophy-like change, or lesions all of the same age. Remember MRI safety contraindications before scanning: certain pacemakers/implanted devices, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips or intraocular metal, and caution with gadolinium in severe renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) and pregnancy.
🎓 Learn the pattern, not just the spots: ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the callosum (Dawson fingers), touching the cortex, in the brainstem/cerebellum, and short-segment in the cord — lesions disseminated in space and time, with gadolinium enhancement separating active from old. That single mental template lets you both diagnose MS and confidently reject its mimics.

Contrast-enhanced MRI (with intravenous gadolinium) is the definitive imaging test for a suspected brain tumour. It characterises the lesion, defines its compartment and margins, guides surgery and radiotherapy, and monitors treatment response — while flagging the emergencies (raised ICP, impending herniation) that change management before any histology exists.

1Why gadolinium — what enhancement means

The normal blood–brain barrier (BBB) excludes gadolinium from the brain parenchyma. Enhancement on post-contrast T1 therefore signals BBB breakdown and/or abnormal neovascularity — leaky, tumour-driven vessels. This is why aggressive tumours light up: high-grade gliomas and metastases recruit disorganised, permeable vessels, whereas low-grade gliomas often enhance little or not at all.

Enhancing lesion on T1+Gad→BBB disruption / neovascularity — think high-grade tumour, metastasis, abscess, or inflammation
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: paired pre- and post-gadolinium axial T1 showing a lesion that is isointense before contrast and avidly enhancing after, illustrating BBB breakdown.
2First reading decision — intra-axial vs extra-axial

Before naming a tumour, decide which compartment it arises from — this halves the differential.

Extra-axial (outside brain substance — arises from meninges, skull, nerves). Signs: broad dural base, dural tail sign, a CSF cleft between lesion and brain, buckling of grey–white matter inwards, vessels displaced rather than encased. Classic: meningioma — usually homogeneous, avidly enhancing, extra-axial.
Intra-axial (within brain parenchyma). Signs: epicentre in the brain, expands the cortex/white matter, no CSF cleft. Classic: glioma and metastasis.
3High-grade glioma (glioblastoma) pattern

The archetypal aggressive intra-axial tumour. Look for a constellation:

GBM→irregular/thick ring enhancement + central necrosis + surrounding vasogenic oedema (bright on T2/FLAIR) + mass effect

It characteristically crosses the midline through the corpus callosum, giving the bilateral "butterfly" appearance. Oedema is vasogenic (spares cortex, tracks white matter) and itself contains infiltrating tumour cells beyond the enhancing rim.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T1+Gad showing a thick, irregular ring-enhancing mass with central non-enhancing necrosis crossing the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma), with FLAIR showing extensive surrounding oedema and midline shift.
4Metastases

Often multiple, sited at the grey–white matter junction (where emboli lodge), typically small enhancing nodules with disproportionately marked oedema for their size. Multiplicity in an adult with a known primary (lung, breast, melanoma, renal, colorectal) strongly favours metastases; a solitary lesion cannot be distinguished from a primary tumour on imaging alone.

5Ring-enhancing lesion — the differential

A ring of enhancement is not specific. Use the mnemonic MAGIC DR:

MMetastasis
Multiple, grey–white junction, marked oedema.
AAbscess
Smooth thin ring; central restricted diffusion on DWI (pus) — the key discriminator.
GGlioblastoma
Thick, irregular ring; necrotic centre; may be butterfly.
IInfarct / Inflammation
Subacute infarct in a vascular territory; gyriform enhancement.
CContusion
Trauma history; typical sites (frontal/temporal poles).
DDemyelination
Tumefactive MS — classically an open (incomplete) ring.
RRadiation necrosis
Prior radiotherapy; mimics tumour recurrence.
Ring lesion + bright central DWI (restricted)→abscess until proven otherwise — most tumours do NOT restrict centrally
6Advanced sequences and clinical role

Perfusion (DSC/relative cerebral blood volume): high-grade tumours and true recurrence show raised rCBV; radiation necrosis is low. MR spectroscopy: tumours show raised choline (membrane turnover) with reduced N-acetylaspartate — a raised choline:NAA ratio; abscesses show amino-acid and lactate peaks instead. These help distinguish tumour grade, tumour vs abscess, and recurrence vs treatment effect.

Clinical role: defines resectability and surgical margins, targets radiotherapy planning volumes, and provides the baseline for follow-up scans assessing response or recurrence.

🚩Raised ICP and the space-occupying lesion. A tumour with mass effect, midline shift, or effaced basal cisterns signals raised intracranial pressure and risk of herniation. Do NOT perform a lumbar puncture when there is a mass lesion or clinical/radiological raised ICP — sudden pressure release can precipitate coning. Give dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema, discuss with critical care if deteriorating, and make an urgent neurosurgical / neuro-oncology referral. Remember MRI safety: screen every patient for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metallic foreign bodies before the scanner, and check renal function before gadolinium.

🎓 When you see a ring-enhancing lesion, your reflex should be two moves: run MAGIC DR and look at the DWI. A thick irregular ring with a necrotic, non-restricting centre crossing the midline is glioblastoma; a thin smooth ring with a brightly restricting centre is an abscess — and that single sequence changes the patient from theatre-for-biopsy to antibiotics-and-drainage.

A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is not a routine head scan. It is a targeted hunt for a structural, potentially resectable epileptogenic focus that a standard sequence can easily miss. The single most important target is the mesial temporal lobe, because hippocampal sclerosis is both the commonest substrate of drug-resistant focal epilepsy and one of the most surgically curable.

1Order the right protocol, not just ‘an MRI brain’

The epilepsy protocol uses high-resolution, thin-slice sequences with a coronal T2 and FLAIR oriented perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus. This orientation lets you compare the two hippocampi side-by-side and detect subtle volume loss and signal change that axial slices blur out.

Routine axial MRI reported ‘normal’→in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, re-request a dedicated thin-slice epilepsy protocol — subtle substrates are often only seen this way
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal oblique FLAIR angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, showing both hippocampi symmetrically for side-to-side comparison.
2Recognise hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis

Hippocampal sclerosis is the classic finding and the substrate of temporal lobe epilepsy. Look for the diagnostic triad on the coronal sequences:

Hippocampal atrophy — asymmetric volume loss on coronal T2
Increased T2/FLAIR signal within the hippocampus
Loss of the normal internal architecture (the interdigitations)

Because it is a well-defined, unilateral, resectable focus, its recognition can lead to a potentially curative anterior temporal lobectomy in appropriately selected patients.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal FLAIR showing a small, bright right hippocampus with lost internal architecture compared with the normal-volume, low-signal left hippocampus.
3Screen for the other resectable substrates

If the hippocampi are normal, the epileptogenic focus may lie elsewhere. Systematically consider these alternative structural causes:

🧠Focal cortical dysplasia
Blurred grey–white junction with a ‘transmantle sign’ (a funnel of signal tapering to the ventricle). A key cause of MRI-‘negative’ epilepsy.
🧬Low-grade tumour
DNET and ganglioglioma — cortically-based, indolent lesions that present with chronic focal seizures rather than mass effect.
🫐Cavernoma
‘Popcorn’ lesion with a haemosiderin rim, best seen on gradient-echo/SWI as blooming low signal.
🩹Gliosis / prior injury
Encephalomalacia or gliosis from old trauma, infarct or infection acting as an irritative scar.
🧱Malformations of cortical development
Heterotopia, polymicrogyria and related dysgenesis — abnormally organised cortex driving seizures.
4Know who actually needs the scan

Not every first seizure needs urgent neuroimaging, but MRI is indicated for new focal seizures, any focal neurological deficit, seizures with atypical features, or established drug-resistant focal epilepsy where surgery is being considered. Finding a resectable lesion is what makes the difference between lifelong medication and a potential cure.

Drug-resistant focal epilepsy→epilepsy-protocol MRI ± referral to a surgical epilepsy centre for pre-surgical evaluation
🚩A first seizure accompanied by focal neurology, persistent focal deficit, or other red flags may signal an underlying tumour or other serious structural pathology and warrants urgent imaging — do not simply reassure. Remember safety counselling: give DVLA driving advice (patients must stop driving and notify the DVLA) and screen for MRI contraindications (pacemaker/incompatible implants, metallic foreign bodies) before scanning.

🎓 The whole point of an epilepsy-protocol MRI is spatial precision: thin coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus turns a ‘normal’ routine scan into a hunt for a resectable focus. Hippocampal sclerosis — atrophy, high signal, lost internal architecture — is the commonest and most curable of these, so in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, if the first scan is negative, question the protocol, not just the patient.

In suspected dementia, MRI brain has two jobs: exclude reversible or structural mimics (subdural, tumour, normal pressure hydrocephalus) and show atrophy/vascular patterns that support a clinical subtype. CT is often the practical first-line scan, but MRI is more sensitive for medial temporal atrophy, small-vessel disease and cortical changes.

1Why we scan at all
Structural imaging is recommended in the work-up of most dementias. The primary aim at UK med-school level is to rule out a treatable or serious structural cause before attributing symptoms to a neurodegenerative process, and secondarily to look for an atrophy or vascular signature that helps type the dementia.
Cognitive decline + need to exclude structural cause→MRI brain (CT if MRI contraindicated/unavailable)
2Atrophy patterns by subtype
Read the scan for where the brain has shrunk and what the white matter looks like.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1 through the hippocampi showing bilateral medial temporal lobe atrophy with widened choroid fissure and temporal horns (Alzheimer's, high Scheltens MTA score).
🧠Alzheimer's disease
Medial temporal lobe / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA score on coronal T1) plus parietotemporal atrophy.
🗣️Frontotemporal dementia
Asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal atrophy (often knife-edge gyri), relative sparring of posterior regions.
🩸Vascular
Small-vessel disease: confluent white-matter hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR, lacunes, and strategic infarcts.
👁️Lewy body dementia
Relatively preserved medial temporal lobe — a useful discriminator from Alzheimer's.
3Exclude the treatable / structural mimics
Before settling on a degenerative diagnosis, actively hunt these on the images:
Subdural haematoma — crescentic extra-axial collection; especially in the elderly/anticoagulated after minor or forgotten trauma.
Tumour — mass, oedema, midline shift; a treatable/serious cause of cognitive change.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, the DESH pattern (disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus). Clinical triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment; potentially shunt-responsive.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial FLAIR showing enlarged lateral ventricles out of proportion to cortical atrophy with tight high-convexity sulci — the DESH pattern of NPH.
4Sequences and safety
Coronal T1 for hippocampal/MTA assessment; T2/FLAIR for white-matter disease and infarcts; DWI for acute infarct and for cortical/basal-ganglia restricted diffusion (cortical ribboning) in CJD. Remember MRI safety: screen for pacemakers/implants, ferromagnetic foreign bodies and cochlear implants, and check renal function before gadolinium.
🚩 Rapidly progressive dementia, focal neurological signs, or young onset warrant urgent imaging — these raise the odds of a reversible or serious cause (tumour, NPH, subdural) or CJD (DWI cortical ribboning). Do not label such a picture as ordinary Alzheimer's without imaging.
🎓 The two questions to ask of every dementia MRI: "Is there something I can treat?" (subdural, tumour, NPH) and "What is the atrophy telling me?" (hippocampal = AD; asymmetric frontal = FTD; small-vessel = vascular; preserved medial temporal = think DLB).

MRI is the imaging modality of choice for suspected CNS infection — it is far more sensitive than CT for early parenchymal change. But imaging never comes before treatment: suspected encephalitis or meningitis is a time-critical emergency where empirical aciclovir and antibiotics are started immediately, before the scanner.

1Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV) — the pattern you must know

HSV-1 encephalitis has a classic limbic distribution. Look for asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling of the medial temporal lobes, extending into the insula and inferior frontal lobes (cingulate involvement common). The basal ganglia are characteristically spared — a sharp boundary at the lateral putamen helps distinguish it from an MCA infarct.

Asymmetric medial temporal + insular T2/FLAIR signal in a confused, febrile patient→Treat as HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise
Restricted diffusion (DWI) — often the earliest change, before FLAIR
Gyral / patchy enhancement post-contrast in later stages
Petechial haemorrhage — low signal on SWI/GRE, a late feature
📷 Image placeholder — Axial FLAIR MRI showing asymmetric hyperintensity and swelling of the right medial temporal lobe and insula, with sparing of the basal ganglia.
🚩Do NOT wait for MRI or CSF PCR to start treatment. In any patient with suspected viral encephalitis, give empirical IV aciclovir immediately — delay increases death and disability. PCR can be falsely negative in the first 24–48 h, and imaging may initially be normal. Treat clinically.
2Cerebral abscess — DWI is the discriminator

A pyogenic abscess is a ring-enhancing lesion with a smooth, thin, regular wall, surrounded by vasogenic oedema. The wall is often thinner along its medial (ventricular) aspect. The single most useful sign is the centre: pus shows central restricted diffusion — bright on DWI, low on ADC.

Ring-enhancing lesion + bright central DWI / low central ADC→Abscess, not necrotic tumour

This is the key exam discriminator: a necrotic/cystic tumour (e.g. glioblastoma, metastasis) usually does not restrict centrally — its necrotic core is facilitated (dark DWI, high ADC) — and tends to have a thicker, more irregular, nodular enhancing wall. Abscess capsule evolution runs early cerebritis → late cerebritis → early capsule → late capsule.

📷 Image placeholder — Paired post-contrast T1 and DWI/ADC images of a ring-enhancing lesion, DWI showing bright central signal with corresponding low ADC confirming pus.
3Meningitis — MRI for complications

In uncomplicated meningitis the MRI is often normal — the diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by CSF. When abnormal, look for leptomeningeal enhancement (best seen on post-contrast FLAIR), following the pial surface into the sulci and basal cisterns (basal enhancement is a clue to TB or fungal meningitis).

Communicating hydrocephalus from impaired CSF resorption
Subdural empyema — extra-axial collection, restricts on DWI
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and venous infarcts
Arterial infarcts from an inflammatory vasculitis
Cerebritis / early abscess formation
4Other patterns worth recognising
🧠Autoimmune / limbic encephalitis
Bilateral medial temporal T2/FLAIR signal without haemorrhage; consider when HSV PCR is negative (e.g. anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1).
🫁CNS tuberculosis
Basal leptomeningeal enhancement, tuberculomas (ring or nodular enhancing), hydrocephalus and infarcts.
🦠Toxoplasmosis (HIV)
Multiple ring-enhancing lesions favouring basal ganglia/grey–white junction; "eccentric target sign".
⚖️Primary CNS lymphoma
The main mimic of toxoplasmosis in HIV — tends to be solitary, homogeneously enhancing, periventricular, and restricts on DWI (hypercellular).
5Safety and the LP rule

A focal neurological deficit, GCS depression, seizures, or clinical signs of raised intracranial pressure mandate imaging before lumbar puncture, to exclude a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus that risks coning. Crucially, this delay must never hold up empirical antibiotics/aciclovir — take blood cultures and treat, then image, then LP. Remember standard MRI safety: screen every patient for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implants and metallic foreign bodies, and weigh gadolinium contrast against renal function.

🎓Two patterns unlock most exam questions: medial temporal + insular FLAIR signal = HSV — give aciclovir now, and central restricted diffusion inside a ring-enhancing lesion = abscess, not tumour. In every scenario, treatment precedes imaging — the scanner confirms, it never gatekeeps therapy.
MRI__Skull Base & Special:
The posterior fossa houses the brainstem, cerebellum and cerebellopontine angles in a tight, bony compartment. On CT, dense petrous and occipital bone throws beam-hardening artefact across these structures, so subtle lesions are easily missed. MRI is the imaging test of choice here — it is unaffected by bone artefact and gives superb soft-tissue contrast for the brainstem and cerebellum.
1Why MRI beats CT in the posterior fossa
CT is fast and excellent for acute haemorrhage, but the surrounding thick bone causes beam-hardening (Hounsfield) artefact that degrades the brainstem and cerebellum. MRI has no bone artefact and superior soft-tissue resolution. Crucially, DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging) detects acute infarcts within minutes, long before they show on CT — vital because posterior circulation strokes are frequently CT-occult. Use CT only when MRI is contraindicated or to exclude acute bleed rapidly.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial DWI showing a bright (restricted diffusion) acute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere/PICA territory.
2Vascular: infarct and haemorrhage
Cerebellar/brainstem infarct (posterior circulation — vertebral, basilar, PICA/AICA/SCA territories) presents with vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria and crossed signs (ipsilateral face, contralateral body). Look for DWI restriction. Cerebellar haemorrhage is a key emergency: an expanding clot compresses the 4th ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus and risks tonsillar/upward coning. Surgical decompression is considered for haematomas >3 cm or with brainstem compression / deteriorating consciousness.
Sudden vertigo + ataxia + DWI restriction in cerebellum→Posterior circulation stroke until proven otherwise
DWI/ADC — acute infarctT2/FLAIR — oedema, chronic changeSWI/GRE — blood productsT1 + gadolinium — tumour enhancement
3Masses: tumours by age
Posterior fossa tumours differ sharply by age. In adults, the commonest are metastasis (often multiple, at grey-white junction) and haemangioblastoma (cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule, associated with von Hippel-Lindau). In children, the classic trio is medulloblastoma (midline, off the 4th ventricle roof), pilocytic astrocytoma (cystic + enhancing nodule) and ependymoma (arises in the 4th ventricle, extrudes through foramina — the "plastic" tumour). Any of these can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.
🧠Acoustic neuroma
Vestibular schwannoma — the commonest CPA lesion. Widens the internal acoustic meatus ("ice-cream cone"); unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.
🧠Meningioma
Second commonest CPA mass. Broad dural base, avid uniform enhancement, dural tail; centred off the meatus (no meatal expansion).
🧠Epidermoid
Insinuates around vessels/nerves; follows CSF on T1/T2 but shows bright restricted diffusion on DWI — the key discriminator from an arachnoid cyst.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T1 post-gadolinium showing an enhancing right cerebellopontine angle mass extending into a widened internal acoustic meatus (vestibular schwannoma).
4Chiari I malformation
Chiari I = cerebellar tonsils herniating >5 mm below the foramen magnum, best seen on sagittal T1/T2. Tonsils become "pointed/peg-like" rather than rounded. It disrupts CSF flow at the craniocervical junction and is associated with a cervical cord syrinx (syringomyelia) — always scan the whole cord. Presents with cough-induced occipital headache, and cape-distribution sensory loss if a syrinx is present.
🚩
A posterior fossa mass or haemorrhage compressing the brainstem or causing acute obstructive hydrocephalus (4th ventricle effacement, dilated temporal horns, transependymal oedema) is a neurosurgical emergency — coning can be fatal within hours. Also remember MRI safety: screen for non-conditional pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, intraocular/intracranial metallic foreign bodies and certain aneurysm clips before scanning.
🎓 Exam pearl. A patient with acute vertigo, ataxia and a normal CT still needs MRI-DWI — up to a fifth of posterior circulation strokes are missed on early CT because of bone artefact and small infarct size. "Normal CT" never excludes a cerebellar stroke.

A dedicated pituitary MRI is a focused, thin-slice study through the sella turcica — not a whole-brain scan. It answers a specific question: is there a lesion in or around the pituitary, and what does it touch? Sequences are coronal and sagittal T1 and T2 at ~2–3 mm, usually with dynamic gadolinium. The trick: a normal gland enhances briskly, whereas most adenomas enhance more slowly — so early post-contrast images make a lesion stand out as relatively dark against the fast-enhancing normal gland.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1 post-contrast through the sella showing a small hypoenhancing focus in the left half of the gland (microadenoma), with the pituitary stalk deviated to the opposite side.
1Orient yourself: sellar anatomy on every scan

Fix three landmarks before hunting for pathology. Above the gland sits the optic chiasm (compression → visual field loss). Laterally on each side lie the cavernous sinuses, carrying the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. In the midline descends the pituitary stalk (infundibulum); a mass often pushes it sideways. The posterior pituitary normally shows a bright T1 spot (stored vasopressin) — its absence is abnormal.

Stalk deviated / gland asymmetric→look for an underlying microadenoma on that side
2Size the lesion: micro vs macro

The single most important measurement is the maximal diameter, because it changes management.

Microadenoma — <10 mm. Confined within the sella. Often found because of a hormone excess (e.g. prolactin). Seen best on dynamic post-contrast images as a slow-enhancing focus.
Macroadenoma — ≥10 mm. Extends beyond the sella: upward (suprasellar, towards chiasm), laterally (into cavernous sinus), or downward. Enhances heterogeneously and may show cystic or haemorrhagic change.
3Functioning vs non-functioning

MRI shows the anatomy; the clinical/biochemical picture tells you what the tumour secretes. Functioning tumours often present small (microadenomas) because symptoms appear early; non-functioning tumours often present large (macroadenomas) with mass effect.

Micro + galactorrhoea/amenorrhoea, high prolactin→prolactinoma (commonest functioning tumour) — treat medically with a dopamine agonist
Coarse features, large hands/jaw, high IGF-1→GH-secreting tumour → acromegaly
Central obesity, striae, high cortisol/ACTH→ACTH-secreting tumour → Cushing's disease
4Mass effect: the chiasm above

A macroadenoma growing upward tents and compresses the optic chiasm. The crossing nasal-retinal fibres (which carry the temporal visual fields) are hit first, producing a bitemporal hemianopia. On the coronal image, look for the mass elevating and flattening the chiasm — the classic "snowman" or figure-of-8 shape as the tumour is waisted by the diaphragma sellae.

Suprasellar extension touching chiasm→formal visual field testing (Goldmann/Humphrey) is mandatory
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1 post-contrast showing a large enhancing sellar mass with suprasellar extension, waisted by the diaphragma sellae into a figure-of-8, elevating and compressing the optic chiasm.
5Pituitary apoplexy — the emergency

Apoplexy is sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary tumour. Clinically: abrupt thunderclap-like headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia (from lateral pressure on the cavernous-sinus nerves), and collapse from secondary adrenal insufficiency. On MRI, acute blood changes signal on T1/T2 — often intrinsically bright on T1 if subacute haemorrhage. This is a time-critical diagnosis.

Sudden headache + visual loss + hypotension→think apoplexy: give steroids first, image urgently, involve endocrinology + neurosurgery
6The main differentials to kill off
ARathke cleft cyst
Benign non-enhancing cyst, often with a small intracystic nodule. Variable T1/T2 signal depending on protein content. Usually incidental.
BCraniopharyngioma
Suprasellar, cystic and solid, calcified (especially in children). Classic paediatric/young-adult sellar mass with visual and endocrine symptoms.
CEmpty sella
CSF herniates into the sella, flattening the gland against the floor. Often incidental; occasionally linked to raised intracranial pressure.
DCavernous sinus invasion
Macroadenoma encasing the carotid or bulging laterally. Predicts incomplete surgical resection and warns of cranial nerve risk.
🚩
Two things must never be missed. (1) Apoplexy with adrenal crisis: a patient with sudden headache, visual loss and shock has secondary adrenal insufficiency until proven otherwise — give IV hydrocortisone immediately, before any imaging delay. (2) Bitemporal hemianopia is chiasmal compression until proven otherwise and demands urgent pituitary MRI and visual fields. And remember MRI safety: screen every patient for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear devices and metallic foreign bodies before they enter the scanner.
🎓 Match the picture to the person: a microadenoma usually declares itself through hormones (prolactin, GH, ACTH), while a macroadenoma usually declares itself through mass effect (headache, bitemporal hemianopia, hypopituitarism). If the presentation is sudden and dramatic, jump straight to apoplexy and reach for hydrocortisone.

MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM) is the gold-standard investigation for unilateral (asymmetric) sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) or tinnitus, ordered to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the cerebellopontine angle (CPA). It is a targeted, thin-slice study of the eighth nerve complex within the IAM and CPA cistern.

1Who gets scanned

Referral is driven by asymmetry. Any patient with unilateral SNHL, unilateral tinnitus, or unexplained one-sided imbalance warrants imaging to exclude a tumour.

Unilateral SNHL / tinnitus / asymmetric audiogram→MRI IAM to exclude vestibular schwannoma
2The protocol

Two complementary sequences give the diagnosis:

High-resolution heavily T2-weighted (CISS / FIESTA): bright CSF fills the IAM so the cochlear and vestibular nerves appear as thin dark strands. A schwannoma shows as a filling defect replacing the bright CSF.
Post-gadolinium T1: a vestibular schwannoma avidly enhances, appearing as a bright soft-tissue mass — sensitive even for small intracanalicular lesions.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial heavily T2-weighted (CISS/FIESTA) at the level of the IAM, bright CSF outlining the nerves, with a soft-tissue filling defect in the left IAM.
3Appearance & origin

A vestibular schwannoma arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII, usually within the IAM. As it grows it extends medially through the porus acusticus into the CPA cistern, producing the classic “ice-cream cone” configuration — the “cone” is the intracanalicular tail in the IAM, the “scoop” is the rounded CPA component.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: post-gadolinium axial T1 showing an avidly enhancing left CPA/IAM mass with the “ice-cream cone” shape, cone tapering into the IAM.
4Symptoms by size

Small / intracanalicular: asymmetric SNHL, tinnitus, and imbalance from CN VIII involvement.

Large (CPA extension): compression of neighbouring structures — CN V (facial numbness, reduced/absent corneal reflex), CN VII (facial weakness — relatively resistant, so weakness is a late sign), and eventually brainstem and fourth-ventricle compression causing ataxia and obstructive hydrocephalus.

5Bilateral disease & differentials

Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic of Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — always inspect both IAMs and consider NF2 in a younger patient.

🧠Vestibular schwannoma
Centred on IAM, “ice-cream cone”, avidly enhancing, expands the porus. Most common CPA mass.
🔵Meningioma
Broad dural base, does not centre on IAM, may show a dural tail and calcification. Second commonest CPA mass.
🍦Epidermoid cyst
Insinuates around structures, follows CSF but restricts on DWI and does not enhance — the key discriminator.
🚩 Never dismiss unilateral or asymmetric SNHL as “age-related” — it must be investigated with MRI IAM to exclude a tumour. A large CPA lesion causing brainstem compression or obstructive hydrocephalus is a neurosurgical emergency. Always confirm MRI safety (pacemaker, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear implant, metallic foreign body) before scanning.
🎓 Bright CSF on CISS/FIESTA acts as a natural contrast agent: a schwannoma is the dark filling defect that lights up avidly on post-gadolinium T1. Remember “ice-cream cone at the CPA = vestibular schwannoma; bilateral = NF2.”

MRI orbits is the workhorse for soft-tissue orbital pathology — the globe, optic nerve and extraocular muscles. It relies on fat-suppressed T1/T2 and post-gadolinium sequences to cut through the bright orbital fat and reveal enhancing lesions. CT still wins for acute trauma, bony orbit and metal foreign body screening.

1Why fat suppression & gadolinium?

Orbital fat is intensely bright on T1, drowning out subtle enhancement. Fat-suppression darkens the fat so an enhancing optic nerve or muscle stands out after contrast.

Bright fat obscures nerve→use fat-sat T1 post-gadolinium
Fat-sat T2/STIR — oedema & inflammation glow bright
Fat-sat T1 + gadolinium — pathological enhancement
📷 Image placeholder — axial fat-suppressed T1 post-gadolinium of the orbits, showing the optic nerves, globes and extraocular muscles against darkened orbital fat.
2Optic neuritis & the MS link

Young patient with painful monocular visual loss and dyschromatopsia (red desaturation). MRI shows a swollen, enhancing optic nerve on fat-sat post-gadolinium images.

Enhancing swollen optic nerve→order MRI brain for demyelination

Optic neuritis is strongly linked to multiple sclerosis. Periventricular white-matter lesions on the brain MRI predict conversion to MS and guide disease-modifying therapy.

3Optic nerve & sheath lesions

Distinguish lesions of the nerve from lesions of its sheath.

Optic nerve glioma — children, association with NF1; fusiform nerve expansion
Optic nerve sheath meningioma — adults; “tram-track” enhancement around a non-enhancing nerve
📷 Image placeholder — axial post-gadolinium image showing “tram-track” enhancement of the optic nerve sheath surrounding a non-enhancing central optic nerve (optic nerve sheath meningioma).
4Thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy)

The classic MRI sign is enlargement of the extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendinous insertions — contrast this with orbital myositis, which involves the tendons.

Fusiform muscles, tendons spared→thyroid eye disease

Mnemonic for muscle involvement: “IM SLO” — Inferior, Medial, Superior, Lateral, Oblique, in decreasing order. The inferior and medial recti are worst affected, and crowding at the orbital apex threatens the optic nerve.

5Infection, tumours & the CT/MRI choice
🦠Orbital cellulitis / abscess
Post-septal spread from ethmoid sinusitis — emergency; look for subperiosteal abscess
🧬Orbital tumours
Lymphoma, metastasis, cavernous venous malformation (“cavernous haemangioma”)
👶Retinoblastoma
Children — leukocoria; MRI stages intracranial & optic nerve spread
🦴CT territory
Acute trauma, bony orbit fractures & metal foreign body screening

Choose the modality by the question: soft tissue and nerve → MRI; bone, blood and metal → CT.

🚩 Vision-threatening emergencies & MRI safety. Compressive optic neuropathy from thyroid eye disease at the crowded orbital apex, and orbital cellulitis with post-septal spread, both threaten sight and need urgent action. On safety: MRI is contraindicated with an intra-orbital ferromagnetic foreign body (e.g. a metalworker with a suspected metal fragment) — the field can move it and blind the patient, so screen with orbital CT/X-ray first.
🎓 Tendon sign splits the diagnosis: extraocular muscle enlargement that spares the tendinous insertions is thyroid eye disease, whereas myositis involves the tendons. And any painful enhancing optic nerve should prompt an MRI brain — you are really screening for MS.
MRI__Head & Neck:
MRI is the workhorse for local (T) staging of head & neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and other neck tumours. Its superior soft-tissue contrast maps depth of invasion, perineural spread, marrow and cartilage involvement, and deep-space extension far better than CT — while CT and PET-CT cover cortical bone, lung and distant disease. Staging is always confirmed and finalised at the MDT, with histology from biopsy.

1Why MRI for T staging

Soft-tissue contrast lets you resolve the tumour edge against muscle, fat and mucosa. Key things MRI shows that change the T stage:

Tumour signal tracks along a nerve into a skull-base foramen→perineural spread — upstages disease, worsens prognosis, alters radiotherapy fields
Loss of normal low-signal cortical rim / abnormal marrow signal→bone or cartilage invasion (e.g. mandible, larynx)
Tongue-base or parapharyngeal fat effacement→deep-space extension — often precludes simple resection
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Axial fat-suppressed post-contrast T1 of an oral tongue SCC: enhancing tumour crossing the midline lingual septum with abnormal marrow signal in the adjacent mandible indicating cortical invasion.
2Sequences that do the work
T1 (non-fat-sat): best for anatomy — bright marrow fat and parapharyngeal fat; loss of this signal flags infiltration.
T2 / STIR: oedema and tumour are bright; helps separate tumour from muscle.
Fat-suppressed post-contrast T1: the money sequence for enhancing tumour, perineural spread and nodal necrosis.
Diffusion-weighted (DWI/ADC): restricted diffusion suggests cellular tumour/malignant node and helps assess treatment response.
3Nodal (N) staging — neck levels I–VI

Cervical nodes are mapped by level (I submental/submandibular, II–IV along the internal jugular chain, V posterior triangle, VI central compartment). Level involvement predicts the likely primary and guides neck dissection. Features that make a node malignant:

📏Size
>1 cm short axis (lower threshold at level II); size alone is unreliable.
⚪Shape
Rounded (loss of normal reniform/oval shape) and loss of fatty hilum.
🕳️Necrosis
Central non-enhancing/necrotic core — highly specific for metastasis.
💥ENE
Extranodal extension — irregular margin, fat stranding; upstages and worsens prognosis.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image. Axial post-contrast T1 showing an enlarged rounded level II node with a central necrotic core and irregular capsular margin, consistent with metastatic nodal disease and extranodal extension.
4Where MRI stops and other modalities start
CT: superior for cortical bone detail and for chest imaging (lung metastases); faster, useful when MRI contraindicated or motion is a problem.
PET-CT: best for an unknown primary (carcinoma of unknown primary presenting with a neck node), detecting distant metastases, and assessing post-treatment response (usually at ~12 weeks).
Ultrasound + FNA/biopsy: tissue sampling — imaging stages, histology diagnoses. Final TNM stage is agreed at MDT.
🚩 A large upper-aerodigestive tumour causing stridor and airway compromise is an emergency — do not send an obstructing patient into a supine scanner. Secure the airway first (senior anaesthetic/ENT help, consider awake fibreoptic intubation or surgical airway). Also watch for impending complications such as carotid encasement (>270° = high blowout risk) and aspiration.
🎓 MRI is unmatched for soft-tissue and perineural spread but demands safety screening — pacemakers, cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies and some clips are contraindications; ask about renal function and gadolinium before contrast. When you read a head & neck MRI, always name the level of any node and hunt for the four malignancy signs: size, round shape, necrosis, and extranodal extension.

MRI is the primary imaging modality for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) — an EBV-associated tumour arising in the fossa of Rosenmüller, far more common in Southeast Asian and southern Chinese populations. It often presents late, and a neck lump or a stubborn unilateral middle-ear effusion may be the only clue.

1Recognise the presentation

NPC hides high in the nasopharynx and spreads early to nodes. The classic ways it declares itself:

Painless upper cervical neck lump (often bilateral)→Cervical/retropharyngeal nodal metastasis — commonly the FIRST sign
Unilateral serous otitis media / conductive hearing loss in an adult→Eustachian tube obstruction by the primary tumour
Epistaxis, blood-stained nasal discharge, nasal obstruction→Local tumour bulk/ulceration
Diplopia, facial numbness, other cranial nerve palsies→Skull-base / cavernous sinus invasion or perineural spread
2Why MRI, and what it shows

MRI is superior to CT for soft tissue and bone marrow, making it the workhorse for local staging. Contrast-enhanced fat-saturated sequences are key.

Primary tumour in the fossa of Rosenmüller and its depth of invasion
Skull-base marrow infiltration — replacement of normal fatty marrow signal (MRI far more sensitive than CT)
Perineural spread along cranial nerves and through skull-base foramina
Extension to parapharyngeal space, cavernous sinus and intracranial compartment
Retropharyngeal and cervical nodal disease, including level and laterality
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: axial T1 post-contrast fat-sat showing an enhancing soft-tissue mass filling the left fossa of Rosenmüller with loss of the normal parapharyngeal fat plane.
3The key MRI signs to name
🎯Fossa mass
Intermediate T1/T2 signal soft-tissue mass in the lateral nasopharyngeal recess, asymmetric mucosal thickening.
🦴Marrow signal loss
Replacement of bright fatty clivus/skull-base marrow on T1 signals early bony invasion.
🧠Cavernous sinus
Superior extension with cranial neuropathy; enhancing tissue tracking through foramen lacerum/ovale.
🔗Retropharyngeal node
Node of Rouvière — the first-echelon drainage station, frequently involved.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image: coronal T1 showing loss of normal high-signal fatty marrow in the clivus/skull base, indicating tumour infiltration.
4From scan to management

MRI defines the T and N stage that feeds the head-and-neck MDT. Diagnosis is confirmed by nasendoscopic biopsy; EBV DNA/serology supports it. NPC is radiosensitive, so treatment is usually chemoradiotherapy rather than primary surgery, with MRI also used for radiotherapy planning and follow-up surveillance.

🚩 Red flags: an adult with unilateral serous otitis media / persistent middle-ear effusion, or new cranial nerve palsies with a nasopharyngeal mass, warrants urgent ENT referral, nasopharyngeal examination and MRI to exclude NPC. Remember MRI safety — screen every patient for pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, cochlear devices and metallic foreign bodies before scanning.

🎓 Pearl: Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult is nasopharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise — never just "grommet and reassure." Look in the postnasal space and image the nasopharynx.

Salivary gland imaging usually starts with ultrasound, but MRI is the workhorse for characterising a gland mass — above all in the parotid. MRI maps the lesion against the facial nerve (CN VII) plane, defines deep-lobe extension, hunts for perineural spread, and screens nodes. Remember the golden rule of size: the smaller the gland, the higher the chance a tumour is malignant.

1Anatomy & the size rule

Three paired major glands — parotid, submandibular, sublingual — plus hundreds of minor glands. Tumour risk flips with gland size:

Larger gland (parotid)→most masses BENIGN (~80%)
Smaller gland (submandibular / minor / sublingual)→rising chance of MALIGNANCY

The key surgical landmark on parotid MRI is the facial nerve plane (retromandibular vein and stylomastoid foramen approximate it), separating superficial from deep lobe.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
2Benign tumours on MRI
Pleomorphic adenoma — commonest parotid tumour. Well-defined, lobulated, strikingly T2 bright. Slow-growing; carries a real risk of malignant transformation if left untreated, so it is excised.
Warthin tumour — older men, smokers; classically can be bilateral / multifocal. Often lower T2 signal with cystic areas; avid on functional imaging.

A well-circumscribed, T2-bright superficial-lobe lesion in a younger patient is the textbook pleomorphic adenoma.

3Malignant tumours & what MRI must report
🧬Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Commonest salivary malignancy. Low-grade lesions mimic benign (well-defined, T2 bright); high-grade are ill-defined with low T2 signal and infiltration.
🕸️Adenoid cystic carcinoma
Notorious for perineural spread — MRI is the best tool to trace tumour along CN VII / V3 to the skull base. Late nodal spread but relentless local recurrence.

Malignant MRI features: ill-defined margins, low T2 signal, restricted diffusion, deep-lobe/skull-base extension, perineural spread, facial nerve involvement and pathological cervical nodes.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
4Inflammatory & non-neoplastic disease
Sialadenitis — diffuse gland enlargement and oedema; acute (bacterial/viral, e.g. mumps) or chronic.
Sialolithiasis — stones, mostly submandibular (Wharton's duct). CT / ultrasound characterise calculi better than MRI; MR sialography shows ductal dilatation.
Sjögren's syndrome — bilateral "salt-and-pepper" / honeycomb glands with mixed cysts; raised long-term lymphoma risk.
HIV — bilateral cystic lymphoepithelial lesions within enlarged parotids.
5MRI safety essentials

Screen every patient before scanning: cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies and certain implants are contraindications. The magnet is always on — enforce zoning and remove loose ferromagnetic objects (projectile risk). Use gadolinium cautiously in severe renal impairment (NSF risk) and pregnancy.

🚩 A parotid mass with facial nerve palsy strongly suggests malignant infiltration until proven otherwise. Pain, rapid growth, fixation to skin/deep tissue, or cervical lymphadenopathy are further red flags mandating urgent referral and tissue diagnosis.
🎓 "Smaller gland, higher malignant odds" — but any facial nerve weakness with a salivary mass overrides the odds and is malignant until disproven. MRI's job is to answer the surgeon's three questions: deep lobe? facial nerve? perineural/nodal spread?

At the skull base, CT and MRI are partners. CT maps the bone and foramina; MRI reveals what CT cannot — marrow signal, soft tissue, dura, cranial nerves and, crucially, perineural tumour spread creeping along nerves through those foramina. Think of MRI as the tool that tells you whether disease has left its compartment.

1Why MRI complements CT

The skull base is a bony floor riddled with holes (foramina) transmitting cranial nerves and vessels. CT gives exquisite cortical detail, but tumour and infection announce themselves first in soft tissue and marrow.

Marrow: normal clivus/petrous apex marrow is bright on T1 (fat). Loss of T1 marrow signal = infiltration (tumour or osteomyelitis).
Perineural spread: MRI's signature strength — look for loss of normal fat in a foramen, nerve thickening and abnormal enhancement on fat-suppressed post-gadolinium T1.
Dura/CSF: dural tails, intracranial extension and CSF leaks are far better seen than on CT.
Foraminal fat replaced + enhancing thickened nerve→perineural tumour spread — this UPSTAGES the cancer
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
2Divide the skull base into thirds

A simple, exam-friendly scheme: anterior, central and posterior. Each has characteristic pathology.

🅰️Anterior (cribriform plate)
Esthesioneuroblastoma, sinonasal tumours with intracranial spread. Watch for CSF rhinorrhoea (dural/cribriform defect).
🅱️Central (sella & clivus)
Clival chordoma, chondrosarcoma, pituitary macroadenoma, meningioma. Cavernous sinus carries CN III–VI and the ICA.
🅾️Posterior (jugular foramen)
Glomus/paraganglioma (classic "salt-and-pepper" signal from flow voids), schwannoma of CN IX–XI.
3Central compartment: the danger zone

The clivus is the midline bone behind the sella. A destructive midline clival mass that is bright on T2 with a marrow-replacing pattern is a chordoma until proven otherwise (arises from notochord remnants). Off-midline, think chondrosarcoma (petro-occipital fissure).

The adjacent cavernous sinus is a crossroads: CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI plus the internal carotid artery run through it. MRI shows tumour encasing the ICA or invading the sinus — findings that change the surgical plan and prognosis.

Midline clival mass, marrow replaced, very bright T2→chordoma
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
4Skull-base osteomyelitis (malignant otitis externa)

Classically an elderly diabetic with severe, unrelenting otalgia and granulation tissue at the external auditory canal. The culprit is usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa, spreading from the ear canal into the skull base and along fascial planes.

MRI finding: replacement of normal bright T1 marrow signal at the petrous apex/clivus with abnormal enhancement of bone and adjacent soft tissue.
Complication: spread to the jugular foramen & hypoglossal canal causes lower cranial neuropathies (IX, X, XI, XII).
Diabetic, severe otalgia, CN palsies, marrow enhancement→skull-base osteomyelitis — treat as an emergency
🚩 Red flag: skull-base osteomyelitis / malignant otitis externa — a diabetic (or immunocompromised) patient with severe otalgia, canal granulation tissue and evolving cranial neuropathies is a serious, potentially fatal infection needing urgent admission, IV anti-pseudomonal therapy and specialist input. Equally, do not miss perineural tumour spread: even a small enhancing thickened nerve upstages the cancer and changes management.
5MRI safety essentials

Before any patient enters the magnet, safety-screen them. The static field is always on.

Ferromagnetic hazards: pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies (e.g. intra-ocular metal in welders) and loose objects that become projectiles.
Gadolinium: check renal function — risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment; caution/consent in pregnancy.
General: claustrophobia, acoustic noise (ear protection), and the need to remove all metal before entry.
🎓 Pearl: When a skull-base cancer patient develops new facial numbness or pain, get a fat-suppressed post-contrast T1 and trace the nerve back through its foramen — MRI catches perineural spread long before CT shows any bone change, and it is often the difference between curative and palliative staging.

MRI is the best test for internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). It is the only modality that directly images the articular disc — the fibrocartilage cushion between the mandibular condyle and the glenoid fossa that is invisible on plain X-ray and CT. MRI answers two questions that drive management: where is the disc? and does it reduce (snap back) when the mouth opens?

1Know the protocol — closed AND open mouth

The TMJ is imaged in oblique sagittal planes (angled perpendicular to the long axis of the condyle) using T1 or proton-density (PD) sequences for anatomy, plus T2 for fluid. Crucially, each joint is scanned in both closed-mouth and open-mouth positions so the disc can be tracked as the condyle translates forwards.

Closed mouth→shows resting disc position
Open mouth→shows whether a displaced disc reduces
2Recognise the normal disc

The normal articular disc is a low-signal (dark) biconcave "bow-tie" structure. On the closed-mouth image the thick posterior band sits at the 12 o'clock position over the top of the condyle. On opening, the condyle translates forward onto the intermediate zone of the disc, which stays interposed between condyle and eminence.

Biconcave low-signal "bow-tie" between condyle and fossa
Posterior band at 12 o'clock (closed mouth)
Disc remains interposed throughout opening
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
3Disc displacement — with vs without reduction

In internal derangement the disc is displaced (usually anteriorly). The key distinction — which determines symptoms and management — is whether it recaptures on opening.

Displaced closed, recaptures on opening→WITH reduction — causes clicking
Stays displaced on opening→WITHOUT reduction — "closed lock", limited opening
📷 Image placeholder — describe the MRI image.
4Look for the other findings

Beyond disc position, systematically check the fluid, bone and marrow.

💧Joint effusion
T2-bright fluid in the joint space; often accompanies acute pain / derangement
🦴Degenerative change
Condylar flattening, osteophytes, subchondral cysts — osteoarthritis of the TMJ
🔥Inflammatory arthritis
Synovial thickening / marrow oedema — e.g. rheumatoid or juvenile idiopathic arthritis
⚪Marrow oedema
Bright condylar marrow on fluid-sensitive sequences — active disease or avascular change
5Put it in clinical context

Temporomandibular disorder (TMD) is common and usually benign: facial pain, clicking, and restricted opening, frequently with a large myofascial component (muscle tension, bruxism). Most patients are managed conservatively — reassurance, soft diet, analgesia, jaw rest, bite splints and physiotherapy — and never need imaging. MRI is reserved for persistent or atypical cases, or when surgery is being considered.

🚩 Not every jaw problem is benign TMD. Progressive trismus, a palpable mass, systemic features of inflammatory arthritis, or pain that seems referred (e.g. from a parotid tumour, nasopharyngeal cancer, or dental/ENT sepsis) all warrant further work-up rather than a TMD label. And remember MRI safety: screen for ferromagnetic implants, pacemakers and metallic foreign bodies before scanning.
🎓 Two images, two questions. The closed-mouth scan tells you where the disc is (posterior band should be at 12 o'clock); the open-mouth scan tells you whether it reduces. Displacement that recaptures = clicking; displacement that stays put = closed lock with limited opening.
MRI__Spine:
MRI whole spine (whole neuraxis) is a sagittal screening study of the entire cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine, usually with axial sequences added through any abnormal level. It is the study of choice when a lesion could sit at multiple levels or when the level is uncertain — because cord compression and metastases are frequently multifocal, imaging only the symptomatic region risks missing disease higher or lower down.
1Know the indications — when "one level" won't do
Request whole spine when disease may be at several levels at once or the level is unknown: suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) with deposits at multiple levels, drop metastases / CSF (leptomeningeal) seeding (e.g. medulloblastoma, ependymoma), multifocal discitis-osteomyelitis, and to localise the level before targeted axial imaging or surgery. A single dermatomal radiculopathy with a clear level usually needs only regional MRI.
Back pain + progressive leg weakness + sensory level + bladder involvement→urgent whole-spine MRI to exclude MSCC / cauda equina
2Read the sequences — what each one shows
Sagittal T1 shows marrow: normal vertebral bodies are bright because of fatty marrow, and metastases replace fat and appear dark (low signal) on T1. T2 / STIR makes fluid, oedema and abnormal cord signal bright — STIR suppresses fat so marrow lesions and soft-tissue oedema stand out. Post-gadolinium T1 is added for tumour, infection and leptomeningeal (CSF-seeded) disease, which enhance. Together these show the level, the cord, and whether the lesion is bone, disc, epidural or intradural.
T1: dark marrow lesion = metastasisSTIR: bright oedema / cord signal changeGad: enhancing tumour, abscess or seeding

3Why whole spine, not just the symptomatic region
Cord compression and metastases are frequently at more than one level. Around a third of patients with MSCC have deposits at multiple non-contiguous levels, and the clinical sensory level often does not match the true compressive level. Imaging only where the patient hurts can therefore miss a second, more urgent lesion — so the whole neuraxis is screened, and any higher lesion may change the surgical or radiotherapy plan.
🦴MSCC (metastatic)
Multiple dark T1 marrow deposits + epidural soft tissue indenting the cord; often multilevel.
💧Discitis / osteomyelitis
Disc + adjacent endplates bright on STIR, enhancing; may be multifocal — screen whole spine.
🌱Drop metastases
Enhancing nodules coating cord/cauda on post-gad T1 — CSF seeding from a CNS primary.

MSCC is an emergency. New or progressive back pain with any neurology — leg weakness, a sensory level, gait disturbance or bladder/bowel dysfunction (also think cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, painless retention) — needs urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, dexamethasone (unless contraindicated) and immediate oncology / spinal surgery referral. 4Check MRI safety before requesting
MRI uses a powerful magnet, so screen for contraindications: non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemakers/ICDs, cochlear implants, certain intracranial aneurysm clips, and intra-ocular or other metallic foreign bodies. Ask about renal function before gadolinium (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe impairment) and about pregnancy. Severe claustrophobia or inability to lie still may need sedation. If MRI is truly contraindicated, CT (± myelography) is the fallback for cord compression.
🎓 Exam pearl. The single best test for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression is whole-spine MRI (T1, T2/STIR ± gadolinium) — because deposits are often multilevel and the clinical level is unreliable. Remember the emergency bundle: MRI within 24h + dexamethasone + urgent oncology/spinal referral.

MRI is the imaging test of choice for the cervical spinal cord and nerve roots. It is the only modality that reliably shows the cord itself — compression, intrinsic signal change, ligaments and discs — and it does so without ionising radiation. Whenever a patient has symptoms or signs pointing to the cord or a cervical root, MRI is the study that answers the question. This subtab walks through how to read a cervical spine MRI and the core pathologies a UK finalist must recognise.

1Orient yourself to the sequences

Start with the sagittal images. On T2, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is bright white, so the cord is outlined by a bright ribbon of CSF front and back — loss of that ribbon means the canal is narrowed. On T1, CSF is dark and fat is bright, giving good anatomical detail of bone and discs. Intrinsic cord damage (oedema, myelomalacia) shows as high T2 signal within the cord itself.

Bright CSF collar around the cord lost over several levels→multilevel canal stenosis — look for cord compression
T2 sagittal — screening sequence; CSF bright, cord compression and cord signal change stand out.
T1 sagittal — anatomy, marrow, disc height; low-signal cord change is subtle here.
T2 axial — confirms cord vs root compression and shows foraminal narrowing.
2Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM)

DCM is the commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults, yet it is frequently missed for months. It is a chronic, progressive squeeze on the cord from age-related degeneration: multilevel spondylosis, posterior disc–osteophyte bars pressing from the front, and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy buckling in from behind. Together these narrow the canal until the cord is compressed, classically at C5/6 and C6/7.

The MRI hallmarks are canal stenosis with cord compression (the cord loses its CSF collar and may be flattened) and high T2 signal within the cord at the compressed level — this represents oedema and myelomalacia and indicates established cord injury.

Clumsy hands, deteriorating balance/gait, Hoffmann's sign, upgoing plantars→suspect DCM — image the cervical cord

Clinically DCM gives upper motor neurone signs below the level (hyperreflexia, spasticity, extensor plantars, positive Hoffmann's) and may show lower motor neurone signs at the level of compression (wasting, absent reflexes in one myotome). Loss of manual dexterity and gait disturbance are the classic early complaints.

3Root, trauma and inflammatory patterns

Not every cervical MRI is myelopathy. Learn to separate cord problems from root problems and to recognise the emergencies.

🤚Cervical radiculopathy
Foraminal disc or osteophyte compressing a single nerve root. Gives dermatomal arm pain, sensory loss and LMN weakness in one myotome. Axial MRI shows foraminal narrowing; the cord is normal.
🚑Traumatic cord injury
MRI shows cord contusion/oedema (high T2) and ligamentous injury that CT cannot see. Essential when neurology is out of keeping with a ‘normal’ CT.
🦴RA atlantoaxial subluxation
Rheumatoid pannus erodes the C1–C2 transverse ligament, allowing subluxation and cord compression at the craniocervical junction. Screen before intubation/GA.
🖐️Central cord syndrome
Elderly patient, hyperextension injury on a spondylotic canal. Arms weaker than legs; central cord T2 signal. Often no fracture.
4MRI safety before you request it

MRI uses a powerful magnetic field, so safety screening is mandatory. Ask about cardiac pacemakers/implantable defibrillators, cochlear implants, intracranial aneurysm clips, metallic intra-ocular foreign bodies, and recent surgery with ferromagnetic implants. Many modern devices are MRI-conditional, but this must be checked with the radiology department — never assume. There is no ionising radiation, which is a key advantage over CT for repeated cord imaging.

🚩 Acute or rapidly progressive myelopathy, and any suspected traumatic cord injury, is a neurosurgical emergency — arrange urgent MRI and immediate spinal referral. Do not wait for outpatient imaging: delayed decompression of a compressed cord risks permanent tetraparesis, bladder and bowel dysfunction.
🎓 If an older patient describes dropping objects, buttons they can no longer manage, and a deteriorating walk, think degenerative cervical myelopathy and get a cervical MRI — high T2 cord signal at a stenotic level confirms the diagnosis and this is the commonest cause of adult cord dysfunction, not a peripheral neuropathy.

The thoracic cord sits in a narrow, rigid canal with a relatively poor ("watershed") blood supply, so it tolerates compression badly. On MRI the thoracic spine is where you hunt for metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC), distinguish benign from malignant vertebral fractures, and pick up cord pathology in a patient with a sensory level. A sensory level on the trunk localises the lesion to the thoracic cord until proven otherwise.

1Read the sequences like a marrow map

Normal adult vertebral marrow is fatty, so it is bright on T1 (brighter than the intervertebral disc). Anything that replaces marrow — tumour, infection, oedema — pushes out the fat and turns the body dark on T1. This is the single most useful rule on the thoracic spine.

T1 — marrow anatomy. Focal/diffuse low signal = marrow replacement (metastasis, myeloma).
T2 / STIR — water. Bright marrow oedema, cord signal change, CSF and epidural disease stand out; STIR suppresses fat so lesions "light up".
Post-gadolinium T1 fat-sat — enhancing tumour, epidural soft tissue, myelitis, dural fistula.

2Metastatic spinal cord compression (the emergency)

The commonest oncological spinal emergency. Vertebral body metastases (breast, prostate, lung, myeloma, renal) grow posteriorly, breach the cortex and form an epidural soft-tissue mass that compresses the cord.

Progressive back pain + leg weakness + sensory level + bladder/bowel change→urgent whole-spine MRI to find all levels of disease

MRI sequence of MSCC: T1-dark marrow deposit → epidural extension → loss of CSF around the cord → cord compression → high T2 signal within the cord (oedema/myelomalacia, a poor prognostic sign). Clinically: a spastic paraparesis with a crisp sensory level and sphincter involvement.

3Benign vs malignant vertebral compression fracture

A wedged thoracic vertebra is a daily problem: is this an osteoporotic fracture or a pathological (malignant) one? MRI settles it.

🦴Benign / osteoporotic
Preserved normal fatty marrow elsewhere in the body; band-like oedema only; retropulsion of a posterior fragment; spared pedicles; no epidural mass; often multiple levels of old collapse.
⚠️Malignant / pathological
Complete T1 marrow replacement of the body; pedicle involvement; convex/bulging posterior cortex; epidural or paraspinal soft-tissue mass; other bony deposits.
4The non-compressive mimics

When the cord is abnormal but not mechanically squashed, think of intrinsic causes:

Thoracic disc herniation — much rarer than lumbar/cervical, often calcified; can still compress the cord and cause a myelopathy.
Transverse myelitis — long-segment, central T2 high signal spanning several segments with cord swelling and patchy enhancement; consider MS, NMO, post-infectious.
Spinal dural AV fistula — the great mimic in elderly men: diffuse lower thoracic cord oedema with serpiginous dorsal flow voids; treatable, easily missed.
🚩 A new sensory level, spastic paraparesis or bladder/bowel disturbance is acute myelopathy / MSCC until proven otherwise. Arrange urgent whole-spine MRI (not just the symptomatic level), start dexamethasone (with PPI cover) if MSCC is suspected, keep the patient flat if unstable, and refer immediately to oncology and spinal surgery/clinical oncology — definitive treatment (surgery or radiotherapy) should be delivered within 24 hours of diagnosis.

MRI safety: always screen for a cardiac pacemaker/ICD, cochlear implant, intracranial aneurysm clips and metallic ocular foreign bodies before scanning. Gadolinium is avoided in severe renal impairment (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) — check eGFR first.

🎓 On the thoracic spine, let the marrow tell the story: bright T1 marrow is your friend. Complete T1 dark-out of a vertebral body with a bulging posterior cortex, pedicle loss and an epidural mass screams malignancy and cord compression — image the whole spine, give steroids, and refer the same day.

Lumbar spine MRI is the imaging of choice for sciatica and suspected radiculopathy, but it is a second-line test: most acute sciatica settles within 6–8 weeks and imaging is reserved for red flags or when surgery is being considered. Remember the anatomy — the spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris around L1/L2, so below this level there is no cord, only the cauda equina and the exiting nerve roots swimming in CSF.
